confidence_note: No full text available; details come from reviews and summaries (Globe and Mail, Core77, reading notes, publisher copy). The old text's conference with 200 people and 15 raised hands, the 40,000-year cave claim and 'brain evolved for images not text' were not found anywhere and were dropped. The Part Three 'start with yourself' advice is a reviewer's paraphrase (low). The last-minute napkin presentation is from a single summary (medium).
facts: In the introduction Roam notes that kindergarteners draw freely while adults do not; adults have forgotten how to express themselves visually.
A summary says Roam found visual thinking when he had to give a last-minute presentation: he sketched a simple framework on a napkin, which clarified his thinking and helped him present.
His claim: any problem can be made clearer with a picture, and any picture can be created with the same set of tools and rules.
Visual thinking needs no artistic skill, only three tools everyone has: eyes (to look), mind's eye (to imagine), hand-eye coordination (to draw and show).
Four steps: look (collect and screen), see (select and clump), imagine (see what is not there), show (make it clear).

In the part on developing ideas, start from a blank napkin and draw the most important element in the middle; for a competitive landscape start with yourself, because you know you are there (reviewer's paraphrase).
Simple hand-drawn sketches help you discover and clarify your own ideas and explain them to others.
The subtitle names two jobs, solving problems and selling ideas with pictures; the book has four parts: an introduction, then discovering, developing and selling ideas.
scene_details: three tools: eyes, mind's eye, hand-eye coordination
most important element drawn in the middle
tension: Adults who draw freely as children now say they cannot draw, yet the book claims they already own every tool needed.
opening_idea: Contrast kindergarteners who draw freely with adults who do not, without naming the author.

lessons.idea: A sketch is a thinking tool, and a rough one is enough.
lessons.anchor: the three tools everyone has and the napkin sketch

reflect_final: Which problem on your desk this week would you understand better after thirty seconds of boxes and arrows on scrap paper?

use_cases.situation: The team talks past each other about a process
use_cases.move: Draw boxes and arrows live, say 'this is how I understand it', and invite corrections.

use_cases.situation: A tangled problem circles in your head
use_cases.move: Remember the three tools (eyes, mind's eye, hand) and put the problem on one sheet before thinking more.

use_cases.situation: A child says 'I can't draw' about a school diagram
use_cases.move: Do an intentionally rough stick-figure version together and see whether it helps explain the idea.

pocket_idea: Rough boxes and arrows on scrap paper are enough to see a problem.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Kindergarteners draw without a worry; adults forgot how, and the book says the tools are still in their pockets.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Roam found visual thinking when a last-minute presentation made him sketch on a napkin; his claim is that eyes, mind's eye and hand are enough.
